title.text: Control mountain descents and animal encounters

why_how.text: The handbook identifies Idaho's traveler service as a source for closures, roadwork, tourism, incidents, delays and weather-related road conditions.
In mountains, heed speed controls and warnings about curves, steep grades and other hazards.
On mountain roads, stay near the right edge to leave space from opposing traffic.
Use a lower gear to control speed on a long downhill grade.
Do not coast downhill in Neutral or with the clutch disengaged.
Watch for a solid yellow line in the lane indicating a mountain-road no-passing area.
Sound the horn before a curve on a narrow road when the view is obstructed.
Do not swerve around a small animal unless certain the maneuver is safe.
For a large animal on or near the road, slow and proceed cautiously because more herd animals may be nearby.
If an animal enters too quickly to avoid safely, consider maintaining control through an impact as the safer alternative.
Livestock being moved under control across a road have priority in Idaho.
When meeting or passing a livestock herd, proceed carefully and cooperate with its handlers.
The handbook describes open range as nearly all land outside city limits and herd districts where livestock customarily or by authorized grazing may roam.
Fences do not establish that livestock are absent or lack priority; use extra caution in open-range areas at night.

Under the handbook's stated open-range or controlled-herd collision rule, an injured or killed animal's owner is not liable for the driver's vehicle damage, and a negligent driver may be liable for the animal.

title.text: Adapt visibility and following space at

why_how.text: At night, keep speed low enough to stop within the road distance actually visible ahead.
Increase the following gap at night.
Use headlights rather than parking lights between sunset and sunrise or when visibility falls below five hundred feet.
At night, watch for unlit or slow vehicles, cyclists, pedestrians and animals.
Allow additional time and distance when passing at night.
Do not begin or continue night driving while tired, and do not wear sunglasses in low light.
Keep both sides of the windshield clean and remove headlight dirt that can weaken or distort the beam.
Avoid staring into approaching headlights; direct the eyes toward the lower right of the driving lane.
Select low beams when approaching or following another vehicle or traveling on a lighted road.
If night parking on a highway shoulder is necessary, use emergency flashers or parking lights.
Keep extra caution around snow-removal equipment because thrown snow can severely restrict a close follower's visibility.

title.text: Work safely around snowplows and low

why_how.text: The winter-driving guidance recommends staying two car lengths behind a snowplow for each ten miles an hour of speed.
Pass a snowplow only when absolutely necessary and when the road ahead is clearly visible; do not pass on the snow-spraying side.
Do not merge back immediately ahead of a snowplow because its blades may be hidden by snow.
Avoid abrupt braking ahead of a snowplow because the heavy vehicle cannot stop as quickly as a car.
Abandon a car during snow clearing only if absolutely necessary, leaving it as far off the road as possible.
Low beams are best in reduced daytime visibility; check that the lights are set low when first switching them on.
Avoid driving in fog, dust storms or heavy rain if possible; if driving is necessary, reduce speed.
Do not use cruise control on a wet or icy road.
Slow further when red taillights appear in poor visibility because the vehicle ahead may be stopped or moving very slowly.

title.text: Respond to rain, hydroplaning and flood

why_how.text: If visibility conditions become too severe, leave the roadway and stop rather than creeping along where another vehicle may strike from behind.
Avoid using emergency flashers while moving in poor conditions because another driver may mistake the vehicle for stopped.
Reduce speed in wet weather because stopping takes more distance and quick turns can cause a skid.
A light rain's beginning can be especially slippery when water mixes with road oil.
Hydroplaning means the tires ride on a water film and can lose roadway contact and control for braking, acceleration or steering.
To reduce hydroplaning risk, slow for rain, slush and standing water, replace worn tires and keep inflation correct.
If entering a slippery area or beginning to hydroplane, keep a straight course and gently release the accelerator.
Do not attempt an abrupt turn or stop while hydroplaning; wait for tire grip to return.
If braking is necessary in the described slippery-area situation, the handbook advises gentle pumping for vehicles without ABS.
Take immediate protective action after a Flash Flood Warning or when water is visibly rising fast.
Do not drive across a flooded road; turn back and select another route.
Leave flood-prone dips, low areas, canyons, dry creek beds and stream corridors for higher, safer ground.
Avoid river, stream and already-flooded areas because an underwater road may have been damaged or washed away.
If a vehicle stalls during the flood situation, leave it promptly and move to higher ground before rising water can sweep it away.
Use added care at night when flooding hazards are harder to see.
During threatening flood conditions, do not camp or park beside a stream or dry stream bed.
The handbook warns that as little as six inches of fast-flowing water can knock a person down, and two feet can carry away a vehicle.

title.text: Use winter control and equipment guidance

why_how.text: On icy or snowy roads, drive slower, turn and stop gently and allow a longer following gap.
Prepare lights, tires, brakes, wipers, defroster and radiator for winter use.
Before even a short winter drive, clean and defrost the windows; keep the washer filled with nonfreezing fluid.
Use the vehicle's fitted safety belts and shoulder restraints during winter travel.
Start slowly to test steering and braking on winter roads, and press the accelerator gently to avoid wheelspin.
The winter guidance says to begin slowing for a turn or stop at least three times sooner than usual.
When stopping on slick winter roads, avoid sudden steering; consult the owner's manual, using gentle brake pumping for non-ABS vehicles and steady pressure when appropriate for ABS.
The handbook recommends tire chains for very slippery roads and checking other states' winter chain rules before traveling there.
Watch for ice in shade and on bridges or overpasses, where it may form earlier or persist longer.
The handbook's usual studded-snow-tire interval is October first through April thirtieth, with possible department changes for weather.

why_how.text: Carry a winter emergency kit in case a breakdown or crash strands the vehicle.
The kit list includes a flashlight and spare batteries, first-aid supplies, a pocket knife and at least one blanket or sleeping bag.
Pack extra gloves, socks, a wool cap, traction sand or cat litter and a small shovel for winter stranding.
Include water, booster cables, emergency flares, nonperishable food, a bright attention cloth, waterproof matches or a lighter, a local map and a phone charger.
Before running the engine for heat while stranded, ensure snow does not block the exhaust pipe.
If available, attach a bright scarf or cloth to the antenna so snow crews can spot the stranded car.
